I've never been much of a reader and I have always credited this to me being a slow reader. I read these articles about these people who claim to read over 300 books in a year -- a rate of almost one l per day, and I can't help but wonder how one could get fast enough at reading to be able to do that.
How can I improve my reading speed?

To me the question is -- does one really want to increase the reading speed? Like check this article.

I think reading means not only trying to absorb the information that is there, but also to reflect on it and form your own thoughts in an ordered fashion. That's the benefit of reading. When one uses this approach, one selects the book to read carefully (more of less) and becomes mentally richer than consuming dozens of books and moving on and forgetting most of they stuff they read.

I can read a book a day when I am not working. The downside to this is that I don't remember most of the books I read for more than a few days and when I do try to remember plots and characters get mixed up. I read A Tale of Two Cities last year and loved it. I was trying to remember details to make a post yesterday and couldn't. Now I have to go back and read it again. I took a speedreading class in highschool and it really helped for textbooks but it is worthless when reading for pleasure.

The more you read, the faster you get at it. You've got a catch 22 for yourself if you don't want to read because it takes you too long. Think of it like just about any other activity. You're more effective with it the longer you keep at it.

You could also try a speed reading program, but the general finding with those is that they greatly lower comprehension.

I guarantee no one who reads 300 books in a year doesn't absorb much. It really boils down to what you want out of reading. Do you simply want to read a buttload of books, or do you want to read more while fully understanding the message? I think finding your own balance is the greatest help. There are tricks, like not subvocalizing and using your peripheral vision. To me, subvocalizing is a huge part of reading, though. Especially if you're reading great prose. Who wants to breeze through lyrical writing? On the other hand, using peripheral vision has really helped me find my balance. It's given my speed a little boost without losing much comprehension. The site already linked should help you with that. But find what works for you and run with it.

Tips:

  1. Intentionally move your eyes across the page faster. Your brain will catch up with your eyes, and you will read more quickly.

  2. Expand your vocabulary. Unfamiliar words slow you down. If you have a larger vocabularly you will get through a book faster.

  3. Don't repeat the words in your head. Some people read aloud in their heads. Squash this habit.

This is pretty much what speed reading is.

Keep in mind that people who say 'I read 300 books last year' may be saying 'I caught a fish, this big...' (in other words, how true is it?)

I think if you are reading the books you want, at a pace where you can swallow them, you should be happy unless you have some kind of learning issue like dyslexia. Books aren't to be consumed like dots in Pac-Man.

I am not a speed reader but the one thing that helped me read at what I consider a normal pace (up from slow) is I practiced processing chunks of sentences at a time and I try my best not to sound out every word in my head unless I am reading a scientific article.

Get a metronome or app of a metronome. There are specific passages you can get but pick a comfortable level of vocabulary for yourself. With metronome on slowest tick, aim to be at the end of each line. Do a few pages over a few days. Gradually increase speed of the metronome. Eventually I am flicking my eyes over three lines roughly from side to side in a z pattern down the text, brain pieces it together. You have to be careful with glossing over bits and as ever, practice it regularly or you lose the edge of it.
